slides: Two more tools that the exam likes. Counting the whole numbers in a range, and the pigeonhole principle.

slides.say: Say a and b are whole numbers, and a is at most b. From a to b, with both ends included, there are b minus a, plus one, whole numbers. You learned this with consecutive integers. For example, from five to twelve, it's twelve minus five, plus one, which is eight numbers.
at: For example, from five to twelve

slides.say: Strictly between five and twelve means both ends are out. That leaves six, seven, eight, nine, ten and eleven, which is six numbers. That's twelve minus five, minus one. So when a is smaller than b, strictly between them there are b minus a, minus one.
at: That's twelve minus five, minus one
So when a is smaller than b

slides.say: With one end in and one end out, it's just b minus a. From five to twelve, with five included and twelve not, that's five to eleven, which is seven numbers.

If you're not sure which rule to use, count a small case on your fingers, like from one to three. And if the answer choices have letters, plug in small numbers, count by hand, and see which choice gives your count.

Now the pigeonhole principle. If there are more items than boxes, at least one box gets two items. Think of four pigeons and three holes. Even if each of the first three pigeons gets its own hole, the fourth one has to share.
at: If there are more items than boxes
Think of four pigeons and three holes
each of the first three pigeons
the fourth one has to share

slides.say: Another example. Thirteen people, and there are only twelve months. Even if the first twelve were born in twelve different months, the thirteenth shares a month with someone. So at least two of them were born in the same month.

On the exam it often comes with remainders. When we divide a whole number by twelve, the remainder is one of twelve options, zero to eleven. These twelve remainders are our boxes, and each number goes into the box of its remainder. So among any thirteen whole numbers, two have the same remainder.
at: So among any thirteen whole numbers

slides.say: And two numbers with the same remainder have a difference that divides by twelve. For example, seventeen and forty-one both leave a remainder of five. Seventeen is twelve plus five, and forty-one is thirty-six plus five. When we subtract, the two fives cancel. That leaves thirty-six minus twelve, which is twenty-four, two times twelve.
